title: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter
description: Learn retry strategies with exponential backoff and jitter. Understand how to retry failures without overwhelming systems.

data.text: Retries are essential for handling transient failures in distributed systems. Exponential backoff with jitter prevents retry storms and helps systems recover gracefully from failures.
Network failures, temporary outages, and rate limits are common in distributed systems. Retries help handle these transient issues.

data.title: Not All Errors Should Be Retried
data.text: Only retry idempotent operations and transient errors. Client errors (4xx) should generally not be retried, and non-idempotent operations need special handling.
Exponential backoff increases the delay between retries exponentially, giving the system time to recover.

data.title: Benefits
data.text: Exponential backoff gives failing services time to recover while preventing immediate retries that could overwhelm the system.
Without jitter, multiple clients retrying simultaneously can cause a thundering herd, overwhelming the recovering service.

items: All clients retry at the same time
Creates load spikes on the failing service
Can prevent recovery instead of enabling it

data.text: Jitter adds randomness to retry intervals, spreading out retry attempts and preventing synchronization.

data.title: Recommendation
data.text: Use full jitter for most cases. It's simple and effective. Decorrelated jitter provides better behavior for very long-running retry scenarios.

items: Set a maximum retry count to avoid infinite retries
Use exponential backoff with jitter for all retries
Distinguish between transient and permanent errors
Implement circuit breakers to stop retries when failing
Log retry attempts for debugging and monitoring
Resource not found (404) unless it's truly transient
When the cost of retrying exceeds the benefit

data.title: Consider the Downstream
data.text: Your retries affect the service you're calling. Implement rate limiting and respect backpressure to avoid overwhelming dependent services.
